My first access to the Internet was as a kid, through Princeton's link to the John von Neumann Computer Network or JVNCnet. I was one of the last people with an email address in the JVNCnet domain. I got access to this when asking schools for help with my independent education, due to chronic health problems preventing me from attending conventional college classes. A professor recommended my use of the Internet to reach other professors to help guide my studies, though this proved futile. Too many other professors, particularly in computing related studies, were resentful of the emerging public access to the Internet they considered their private domain and refused to communicate with 'non-paying customers'. That's the real attitude of most American academics. Still, I had free modem-speed access to the very early Internet for some years.

Before the Web, most Internet activity revolved around email mailing lists, Usenet, open FTP servers hosting file libraries, and the Gopher search tools used to explore them. For a long time hopes of a truly useful Internet rested on Ted Nelson's Xanadu project, but it never reached a critical mass. For a long time I dreamed of opening my own SilverStand--what we would later refer to as an Internet Cafe.

The early growth of public use of the Internet emerged with the advent of 'terminal servers' which afforded a lower cost means of providing an Internet gateway with access for many modems. For a long time accessing the internet required dedicating a workstation class computer to serving modem connections, with the maximum number of them per machine being around a dozen. The terminal server expanded this to many dozens and eventually eliminated the need for a control computer. This catalyzed the emergence of 'net wallahs'; small regional ISPs whose businesses leveraged Internet access negotiated, at first, through friends in universities. Some of these small businesses grew and persisted but most were destroyed when the US Congress finally woke up to the existence of the Internet and conservatives decided to 'gift' it wholesale to the few largest telecom corporations.

Then CERN unleashed the Web on the world and the public Internet really took off. The Web was originally simply an on-line Hypertext platform--which was also an invention of Ted Nelson's. (I was long a user of stand-alone hypertext systems and still use them as a general writing tool to this day) Early web use relied on bookmarks and cross-linking, as, unlike Xanadu, it lacked an integral mechanism for indexing. Early search sites like Yahoo at first relied on manual tabulation of web content into simple categories, like searching a library catalog. Seems ridiculous now, but there weren't that many sites on any particular topic at first. Getting access to server space for a web site was expensive and sometimes still impossible outside universities. These search sites built their business models on trying to be the default 'home page' of the Internet, creating a comprehensible default starting point for users given that the net was still something of a Tokyo in a black-out searched with a flashlight experience. And, of course, the screen real estate of a default home page for the net had value as ad space. Web rings were also popular, particularly with sites relating to fandoms. These were based on a simple script that would let web sites of a common topic pool together in a ring so when a user clicked on the ring banner on a page it would take them, sequentially, through all the sites that joined the ring.

Soon, however, ISPs began offering web hosting as a basic part of a net subscription, hawking the idea that every person, family, or business needed a web page. Web sites proliferated rapidly and web search automation became critical, demanding new technology that created an opening for companies like Google whose rise was meteoric. A dot-com boom emerged as ever-gullible investors began throwing money at anything Internet related in the hopes of reproducing the Google success, and that brought us to the hyper-commercialized internet we know today.

This is the most important computer tip.

Start using free software. That is free, as in freedom, not free, as in beer. Free software RYF (Respects Your Freedom). If you do decide to switch to free software, it really helps if you have free hardware, too. You can check if your hardware is free here:

h-node

Free Operating System
* Trisquel GNU/Linux - Easier if you are new, and soon due for a big update. :)
* Parabola GNU/Linux - More difficult to install, but very modern. Have a friend help.

Free Hardware

Think Penguin - Based in the USA and UK, they know and love freedom, have a mission to support the free culture ecosystem and will ensure that your hardware will software will work well.

Minifree - A completely and utterly free computer, even down to the BIOS level, which uses LibreBoot.

EOMA68 - free hardware, currently crowd funding.

If you are interested in freedom, check out the GNU pages and philosophy. Remember to use "GNU+Linux", not simply "Linux". GNU is all about freedom. "Open Source" is about convenience.

I have already purchased a new computer with a touch-screen and await its arrival; I discussed the subject with my uncle, a former engineer, and he suggests and I agree that I should abandon Windows in its actual form and install Linux. I am personally rather concerned by the data collection that Microsoft, and presumably espionage agencies through the world, involve themselves in.

However, I am not a peculiarly technically inclined person. I can browse anonymously and resolve simple errors yet when I search for information on how to install Linux, I find only confusing discussions of kernels and partitions and other terms that I have scarcely encountered before. I understand that the Linux family of operating systems was traditionally intended for those skilled with computers. However I do not believe that Microsoft and the United States need know whenever I have opened a picture of my cat, and have heard many other bad things of Windows 10.

How can I choose and install a desktop distribution of Linux to my new computer when it arrives? I am certain that there must be some way that I can do so.

1) How can I install GNU+Linux? (Please remember to say GNU+Linux. It helps you and others keep freedom in mind.)

These days, it is surprisingly easy to do. Basically:

1) Download a file (It is a large file, and the format is usually .iso This file is the Operating System, for example Trisquel GNU/Linux)
2) Create a live, bootable USB drive. (Do you have an 8GB USB drive/pen drive? This will do. RMprepUSB and then Easy2Boot is the most convenient way at the moment, but you may find it confusing, if you are inexperienced. Newbies ought to try Unetbootin.)
3) Boot from your Live USB (In your BIOS settings, you will need to tell your computer to boot from your USB drive, rather than your hard disk, or your DVD.)
4) Install from Live USB to your hard disk (Your computer will actually be running GNU+Linux during this process. Hopefully, your hardware is free and your ethernet, card for wired internet, and your wireless card, for wi-fi, are working. This stage puts the OS (Operating System) onto your computer. It is the equivalent of installing (yuch!) micro$oft windoze from a DVD.)
5) Boot and use GNU+Linux Welcome to freedom!

  • Try and find a GNU buddy! There are install fests, and LUGs (Linux User Groups). Defer to the person who says "GNU" or "Libre". They care about freedom.
  • DTE (Desk Top Environment) - Start with KDE. Stick with it a while, and become fluent with its interface. Then, when experienced, try out some other ones, like LXQT.
  • Linux is non-free. (It contains binary blobs.) Use the free kernel, LinuxLibre.
  • AskUbuntu is a good site to find answers to questions.
